title: (Mis)Information on Digital Platforms: Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis of Content From Twitter and Sina Weibo in the COVID-19 Pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of COVID-19 posts on Twitter and Sina Weibo on two dates (30 Jan and 6 Feb 2020). Human coders classified a random subsample of keyword-matched posts as misinformation or not, adjudicating accuracy against the WHO Mythbusters fact-check page, and report the share of posts that were misinformation on each platform (1.1% Twitter, 0.3% Weibo). These are CONTENT shares of items that exist in a keyword corpus, with stated numerators and denominators.

estimates.country: Twitter, described by the authors as 'based in the United States'; posts were selected by English keywords with no geographic filter and non-English posts were discarded
estimates.date: 30 January 2020 (within 24 h of the WHO PHEIC declaration) and 6 February 2020; the extracted value pools both dates
estimates.measure_type: % of English-language coronavirus/COVID-19 keyword tweets that were coded as containing COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 1.1% of tweets: 5 (0.7%) of 746 tweets in batch 1 and 6 (2.8%) of 211 tweets in batch 2 (11/957)
estimates.denominator: 957 English-language tweets manually coded (746 in batch 1 + 211 in batch 2), drawn as a 5%-7% random selection of an initial 1% random sample of 2,344,322 keyword-matched coronavirus/COVID-19 tweets
estimates.definition: Post manually coded as containing misinformation, with accuracy calls adjudicated against the WHO COVID-19 Mythbusters fact-check page
estimates.misinfo_def: “misinformation, defined as incorrect information that is not intentionally false”
estimates.source_quote: We found that 1.1% of tweets from Twitter contained misinformation on COVID-19, with 5 (0.7%) of 746 tweets after discarding non-English posts in batch 1 and 6 (2.8%) of 211 tweets after discarding non-English posts in batch 2, compared to 0.3% on Weibo, with 1 (0.4%) of 279 posts in batch 1 and 1 (0.2%) of 441 posts in batch 2—a higher level of misinformation by a factor of almost 4 in the 1-week period on Twitter compared to Weibo.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three coders independently read and classified posts using Fung et al.'s topic classification, then the team recoded to verify alignment and the lead coder did a final review and deconfliction; accuracy calls adjudicated using the WHO COVID-19 Mythbusters fact-check website. NO inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa or percent agreement) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The first batch of posts consisted of a 1% random sample of Tweets and Weibo posts created within 24 hours of the WHO declaration ... The second batch was a 1% random sample of Tweets and Weibo posts created 1 week after the WHO declaration (February 6, 2020), both searching English keywords “coronavirus” and “covid-19” and the Chinese words “新冠,” “新型冠状病毒,” and “疫情.”
estimates.notes: Two batches (30 Jan and 6 Feb 2020) collapsed to the paper's own pooled headline figure (1.1%); the per-batch values differ fourfold (0.7% vs 2.8%) on extremely small numerators. The numerator is 11 tweets in total, so the estimate is very imprecise; the paper reports no confidence interval. COUNTRY: the authors frame Twitter as the US platform, but sampling was by English keyword with no geographic restriction, so this is coded Global rather than United States - a country-level user of this row should not read it as a US estimate. The coded misinformation tweets (Textbox 1) include speculation, jokes and conspiracy talk as well as clearly false claims, so the label is applied more loosely than the stated WHO-fact-check standard.

estimates.country: China (Sina Weibo, Mandarin-language posts from the Weibo-COV corpus)
estimates.date: 30 January 2020 and 6 February 2020; the extracted value pools both dates
estimates.measure_type: % of Chinese-language coronavirus/COVID-19 keyword Weibo posts that were coded as containing COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 0.3% on Weibo: 1 (0.4%) of 279 posts in batch 1 and 1 (0.2%) of 441 posts in batch 2 (2/720)
estimates.denominator: 720 Chinese-language Weibo posts manually coded (279 in batch 1 + 441 in batch 2), drawn as a 5%-7% random selection of an initial 1% random sample of 1,235,243 keyword-matched Weibo posts
estimates.definition: Post manually coded as containing misinformation, with accuracy calls adjudicated against the WHO COVID-19 Mythbusters fact-check page
estimates.misinfo_def: “misinformation, defined as incorrect information that is not intentionally false”
estimates.source_quote: compared to 0.3% on Weibo, with 1 (0.4%) of 279 posts in batch 1 and 1 (0.2%) of 441 posts in batch 2—a higher level of misinformation by a factor of almost 4 in the 1-week period on Twitter compared to Weibo.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same procedure as the Twitter sample: three coders (three team members fluent in Mandarin, two native speakers) coded independently, team recoding for alignment, lead-coder deconfliction, accuracy adjudicated against the WHO Mythbusters page. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: With respect to Weibo, we used a large-scale COVID-19 social media data set that includes a total of over 40 million Weibo posts [20]. The data set, Weibo-COV, covers posts from December 1, 2019, to April 30, 2020
estimates.notes: Numerator is TWO posts in total (one per batch), so the 0.3% is essentially a single-observation rate; the authors themselves caution that 'we cannot eliminate the possibility that more misinformation existed but was just removed quickly' by Weibo moderation, which is a direct threat to this estimate's interpretation as prevalence of produced content. Both of the coded Weibo 'misinformation' posts are traditional-Chinese-medicine/immunity content (Table 3), i.e. the label rests on guideline-discordance rather than on a specific fact-checked false claim.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) 'Twitter reported that 0.3% of election-related tweets were flagged as misinformation [24]' - a figure the paper cites from elsewhere; R8 bars figures cited from another source. (b) Table 1/Table 2 keyword and hashtag frequencies and relative risks - these are term frequencies, not veracity classifications. (c) The per-batch values (Twitter 0.7% and 2.8%; Weibo 0.4% and 0.2%) are kept inside value_raw rather than split into separate rows, because the two dates are a two-point time series one week apart and the paper's own headline is the pooled figure; splitting would create four rows on numerators of 5, 6, 1 and 1 posts. (d) The raw-data split of posts across batches (e.g. 491,353 (39.78%) of Weibo posts in batch 1) is a within-corpus volume distribution, not a misinformation share.

rob.design: Cross-platform content analysis. Twitter: academic API keyword search ('coronavirus', 'covid-19') on two dates, 2,344,322 tweets, 1% random sample, then a 5%-7% random subsample manually coded (954 of 15,737 in batch 1 and 448 of 7,726 in batch 2, reduced to 746 and 211 after discarding non-English posts). Weibo: Weibo-COV corpus (>40 million posts, Dec 2019-Apr 2020) searched with Chinese equivalents, 1,235,243 posts, same 1% then 5%-7% sampling (279 and 441 coded posts). Three coders classified independently, followed by team recoding and lead-coder deconfliction; accuracy adjudicated against the WHO Mythbusters fact-check page. No inter-rater reliability statistic is reported anywhere. Total misinformation numerators are 11 tweets and 2 Weibo posts; no confidence intervals. Weibo content moderation/censorship is an acknowledged, unquantified downward bias on the Weibo estimate.
rob.item6_quote: In addition, we determined whether tweets and Weibo posts contained sources of misinformation through our manually coding and categorizing of the randomly selected subdata sets. Specifically, we manually categorized microblog contents under different themes to identify the information and misinformation, using the WHO fact-check website to adjudicate accuracy calls [8].
rob.item10_quote: We found that 1.1% of tweets from Twitter contained misinformation on COVID-19, with 5 (0.7%) of 746 tweets after discarding non-English posts in batch 1 and 6 (2.8%) of 211 tweets after discarding non-English posts in batch 2, compared to 0.3% on Weibo, with 1 (0.4%) of 279 posts in batch 1 and 1 (0.2%) of 441 posts in batch 2.
